A common path is to start in rehabilitation / nursing, work as a therapy assistant, earn qualifications and practice under a therapist, independently lead training groups, and advance to therapy team leader or transition into an occupational therapist role.
This work suits gentle, patient, hands-on people willing to coexist with injury and illness. If helping people regain independence feels meaningful, this can be a stable career.

paragraphs: In the morning, receive patients, review daily plans, and practice using spoons and dressing. At midday, organize medical records and progress charts and discuss adjustments with therapists. In the afternoon, lead group game-based training and support patients emotionally. Before leaving, organize the next day's schedule and return equipment to its place.

In short, they put rehabilitation plans into practice with patients. Work includes leading movement training, recording progress, teaching assistive devices, arranging daily-living exercises, maintaining the environment, and reporting changes. Combining practical work with empathy, they implement rehabilitation on the front line.

This work suits people who combine gentleness + patience + hands-on ability. Training must produce results and continue over time, requiring a balance of professional technique and emotional support.

This work develops professionalism through patience. Assistants must understand movement training and human function while providing emotional support. It suits gentle, patient people willing to watch gradual improvement and who enjoy helping patients progress from guided practice to independence.
Prefers helping, practical, and investigative work (Social S + Realistic R + Investigative I).

The greatest career risk is not AI but staffing and authorized positions. Demand rises while positions remain limited, and qualified people with strong companionship skills become more secure.

The greatest occupational risk is not AI but staffing and authorized positions. Rehabilitation demand rises while frontline staffing remains tight, and digital tools redistribute some assessment work. Hands-on training still requires people.

No matter how intelligent robots become, assistants still use their hands, encouragement, and steadiness to judge which steps a patient can take, motivate progress, and adapt training to the person. People cannot be removed entirely from rehabilitation.
In short, the future shortage is not of people who record data, but of occupational therapy assistants who are patient, sustain training, and guide it accurately.
